questions.prompt: Which one of the following most accurately describes the author's main purpose in the passage?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
For primary purpose questions, we often use our **Framework** as a good starting point for a pre-phrase.

We probably would have used an *Old / New* or *Answer a Question* framework for this passage.

The underlying question is, "What accounts for superior performance? (How does someone like Simone Biles get that much better than everyone else?)"

The *Old* answer was ... "She's born with innate talent!"

The *New* answer that comes from "recent research in different domains of excellence" says ... "You need a minimum baseline of skill / physical attributes to qualify, but from there, it's way less about innate talent and way more about how much training and practice you do (and how that training / practice imparts physiological changes on you)."

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body: We want something like, "The purpose of the passage was **to present a new answer to the question of what causes superior performance.**"

choices.text: to illustrate the ways in which a revised theoretical model can be applied to problematic cases for which previous versions of the theory offered no plausible explanation
choices.explanation:
We *are* revising our model (or more properly, our understanding) of what causes superior performance.

We used to think it was innate talent. Now we think it has more to do with sustained high-level training.

According to this answer, most cases of superior performance were always explainable via the "innate talent" hypothesis, but there were some lingering problematic cases where they didn't have innate talent but did have superior performance.

This revised theory (that says superior performance is more about sustained high-level training) can account for these problematic cases.

But this passage wasn't saying, "we've revised the theory that *innate talent causes superior performance*" and then showing us examples of previously problematic cases that can now be explained.

The passage was saying, "we're getting rid of that old theory that tried to explain most cases of superior performance as the result of innate talent, and we're replacing it with an understanding that most cases of superior performance are the result of sustained high-level training".

choices.text: to argue that the evidence that was previously taken to support a particular theory in fact supports an opposing theory
choices.explanation:
This passage didn't say, "we ran the numbers again on this same evidence and arrived at a different conclusion".

Rather, it said, "Until recently, however, little systematic research was done on the topic of superior performance .... **Recent research** in different domains suggests that ..."

So the old theory was based on skimpy / little evidence. The new theory is based on brand new research.

choices.text: to show how a body of recent research provides evidence that certain views based on earlier research are not applicable to a particular class of cases
choices.explanation:
This answer is an unlovable disaster that just ends up being our "best available".

It's lovable in the very general sense that it conveys the right sense of "New research goes against old idea".

But the details take a lot of "making peace" with.

Is there "a body of recent research"?

Yes, the 2nd paragraph's second sentence tells us that "recent research in a different domains of excellence suggests that superior performance arises predominantly from acquired complex skills and physiological adaptations, rather from innate abilities".

Is this research finding "evidence that certain views based on earlier research are not applicable to a particular class of cases"?

The view based on earlier research was that "superior performance is caused by innate abilities", so yes this old view and this body of recent research definitely conflict; one is not **applicable** to the other.

What was the earlier research that the Old view was based on?

There was data concerning prodigies and the apparent heritability of relevant traits. There were examples of superior musicians, most of whom were already standouts by age six (suggesting innate gifts).

What is the "particular class of cases" that the body of new research is dealing with?

Our 2nd sentence of the 2nd paragraph just says, "in different domains of excellence". That's vague, but it is a particular class of cases.

The passage also uses some specific examples, such as accomplished athletes and accomplished chess players.

Overall, the "particular class of cases" gives off this vibe that the author was saying, "Superior performance is caused by intense training, *within these specific fields*", whereas the passage felt more like it was saying, "In general, superior performance is caused by intense training".

This seems to be a totally unnecessary flourish the test writer chose in order to make this answer less attractive.

choices.text: to defend the author's new interpretation of data against probable objections that might be raised against it
choices.explanation:
The author just presents a new way of accounting for superior performance, based on recent research data.

There aren't any "potential objections" raised and addressed.

choices.text: to explain how a set of newly formulated abstract theoretical postulations relates to a long-standing body of experimental data in a different, but related, field of inquiry
choices.tag: Out of Scope: set of new postulations
choices.explanation:
This answer sounds way too technical for the fuzzy, real-world science we're talking about here.

We're just wondering if Tiger Woods has some special innate gifts or just got insanely better than everyone else because he trained harder and practiced more.

We don't have any abstract, theoretical postulations.

The closest we have to that is one solitary postulation:
*exceptional performance arises predominantly from acquired complex skills and physiological adaptations, rather than from innate abilities*

We definitely don't connect this one postulation to a **long-standing** body of evidence, since the Old theory was weakly supported ("little systematic research was done") and the New theory has **recent** research.

*~typical config → ~exceptional memory*

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body: We want an answer that sounds like "a configuration of chess pieces that isn't typical for the game of chess".

choices.tag: Out of Scope: sequences of moves
choices.explanation: We're looking for "configurations of pieces" (i.e. where the pieces are distributed on the board), not the way they move from space to space over the course of a sequence of moves.

choices.tag: Out of Scope: complex sequence w/o spatial
choices.explanation: We have a really narrow support idea to work with (atypical configuration of chess pieces), and so if the language of the answer isn't anywhere near that, we're moving on.

We have a really narrow support idea to work with (atypical configuration of chess pieces).

We were looking for "atypical configurations of chess pieces".

Configuration = arrangement

So this matches what the passage told us. Superior chess players do ****not**** have exceptional memory for some kinds of arrangements of chess pieces (the kind of arrangements they don't have good memory for = arrangements that do not typically occur during chess games)

We have a really narrow support idea to work with (atypical configuration of chess pieces).

"Factors requiring logical analysis in the absence of competition" doesn't sound anything like "the pieces are placed on the board in a weird way that usually wouldn't happen during a chess game".

passages.title: Explaining Mirror Images
passages.text:
Physicists are often asked why the image of an object, such as a chair, appears reversed left-to-right rather than, say, top-to-bottom when viewed in a mirror. Their answer is simply that an image viewed in a mirror appears reversed about the axis around which the viewer rotates his or her field of sight in turning from the object to its reflected image. That is, the reversal in question is relative to the position and orientation of the observer when the object is viewed directly. Since we ordinarily rotate our field of sight about a vertical axis, mirror images usually appear reversed left-to-right. This is the field-of-sight explanation.

However, some physicists offer a completely different explanation of what mirrors “do,” suggesting that mirrors actually reverse things front-to-back. If we place a chair in front of a mirror we can envision how its reflected image will appear by imagining another chair in the space “inside” the mirror. The resulting reflection is identical to, and directly facing, the original chair. The most notable thing about this explanation is that it is clearly based on a false premise: the chair “inside” the mirror is not real, yet the explanation treats it as though it were as real and three dimensional as the original chair.

This explanation appeals strongly to many people, however, because it is quite successful at explaining what a mirror does—to a point. It seems natural because we are accustomed to dealing with our mental constructs of objects rather than with the primary sense perceptions on which those constructs are based. In general, we can safely presume a fairly reliable equation between our perceptions and their associated mental constructs, but mirrors are an exception. They present us with sense perceptions that we naturally construe in a way that is contrary to fact. Indeed, mirrors are “designed” to make a two-dimensional surface appear to have depth. Note, for example, that mirrors are among the few objects on which we almost never focus our eyes; rather, we look into them, with our focal lengths adjusted into the imagined space.

In addition to its intuitive appeal, the front-to-back explanation is motivated in part by the traditional desire in science to separate the observer from the phenomenon. Scientists like to think that what mirrors do should be explainable without reference to what the observer does (e.g., rotating a field of sight). However, questions about the appearances of images can be properly answered only if we consider both what mirrors do and what happens when we look into mirrors. If we remove the observer from consideration, we are no longer addressing images and appearances, because an image entails an observer and a point of view.

summaries.standard:
****Topic****

Why mirrors appear flipped left-to-right

****Framework****

Challenge a Position / Present a Debate / Explain Something Curious

****Main Point****

The front-to-back explanation of what mirrors do, unlike the field-of-sight explanation, is faulty because the 'behavior' of mirrors is dependent on an observer, which that explanation fails to capture.

****Summary****

*P1 - The Standard Explanation (field-of-sight)*

The passage begins by explaining how physicists answer the question of "why images appear reversed left-to-right in mirrors". Their explanation is called the field-of-sight explanation and holds that, "*the reversal we see in the mirror is based on the axis we're using to turn our head from the mirror to the object and back again."* It's not clear in realtime that the author endorses this explanation.

*P2 - The Alternate Explanation (front-to-back)*

We begin with a PIVOT (however), so this seems very important. Is *this* the author's preferred explanation? We find out that the author has at least some problems with it towards the end of the paragraph, when she points out that it's based on a false premise that it treats as though it's a real thing.

*P3 - Explaining the Appeal / the Problem with the Alternate Explanation*

The author begins by making some sympathetic concessions -- "guys, guys. i get why people like hearing this explanation, and that's probably why some physicists like giving the explanation".
- *appeals because it's successful to a point*
*- it seems natural to trust our mental constructs*
*-* *****but mirrors are an exception!*****

*P4 - Continuing to explain the Appeal / the Problem*

This paragraph also discusses why this front-to-back explanation can be appealing before discussing her ultimate problems with it. How are P3 and P4 different? P3 is more about why regular people would like it but should think twice about it. P4 is more about why scientists would like it but should think twice about it.
- *yes, it's nice that this explanation removes the observer from the phenomenon, as we aim to do in science.*
*-* *****However,***** *we're trying to explain why mirrors* *****appear***** *as they do, which is nonsensical to speak of how they appear unless there's an observer perceiving them.*

****Commentary****

I found this passage a tricky read, in terms of guessing where the author was ultimately landing. She never explicitly indicates that she likes the field-of-sight explanation, but since it *does* explain mirrors in relation to the observer, she presumably would be fine with it.

When you re-read the first paragraph and beginning of the 2nd thinking that she likes field-of-sight and doesn't like front-to-back, you might notice that the first paragraph is attributed to ****physicists****, like the whole group, the mainstream, the standard.

The second paragraph is attributed to ****some physicists****, which we might ultimately come to think of as the exceptions, the outliers, the rogue physicists. Our author apparently wants to explain why their thinking is whack

We could think of this passage as a Debate, since there are two different points of view on how to explain how mirrors appear (and author chooses Side A).

We could think of it as Challenge a Position, with the author challenging the front-too-back explanation.

Or we could think about it as Explain Something Curious, the curious thing being how mirrors seem to flip the left/right image of an object in the reflection. Paragraph 1 and 2 each give a separate Explanation, and the author discusses the appeal but the ultimate problems with the second Explanation.

questions.prompt: The main point of the passage is that an adequate explanation of mirror images

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
This isn't a conventional Main Point question, since it pre-loads the first half of the main point sentence.

So we can do some proactive thinking here. Where was the author saying what would make for an ****adequate**** explanation?

We know the author's voice didn't really show up until the final paragraph, especially after the Purpose
Pivot (but, yet, ****however,**** recently) in the second to last sentence.

*Questions about appearances of images can be* *****properly answered only if***** *...*

This means the same thing as
*an* *****adequate explanation***** *for the appearances of images in a mirror* *****requires***** *...*

The author says that an adequate explanation must consider what mirrors do and what happens when we look into mirrors.

So we're looking for an answer we can match up with "what mirrors do and what happens when we look into mirrors".

choices.text: must include two particular elements
choices.explanation:
This is a silly answer, in terms of how unnecessarily vague it is, but it *does* match up with the text we need it to match up with:

*what mirrors do and what happens when we look into mirrors*

Questions about mirrors can only be adequately addressed if we consider both

1)
and
2)

choices.text: has yet to be determined
choices.tag: Out of Scope: yet to be determined
choices.explanation:
The author never officially endorses the field of sight explanation, but she never pushes back on it, so it's she is implicitly accepting it.

The first sentence says "Physicists are often asked X. Their answer is simply Y." This presentation suggests that Y is the standard, accepted answer to the question.

The second paragraph is saying "*some* physicists offer a completely different explanation". This quantifier makes this position seem more like the fringe position. And it is this explanation that our author is ultimately writing this passage for. She is expressing her displeasure with this alternative explanation, since it leaves out the observer.

The field of sight explanation *includes* an appreciation of the observer, so we have no reason to think the author is dismayed by the field of sight explanation. And since it's presented as the more default, accepted answer provided by "Physicists", the author might be thinking, "THIS explanation is fine. THIS OTHER one called front-to-back is whack."

choices.text: must be determined by physicists
choices.explanation: We don't have any support for the idea that the author thinks that an adequate explanation of mirrors ****has**** to be done by a physicist. Someone who specializes in optics or metals or geometry might be equally qualified to provide an adequate explanation.

choices.text: is still subject to debate
choices.explanation:
The author would agree that an adequate explanation is still subject to debate, since she presents a debate of alternate explanations.

However, her main point is not that "an adequate explanation is still up for debate". She had a more targeted purpose (we used a Challenge Position framework), so that needs to be expressed in the Main Point.

Her Main Point is essentially "this other explanation being debated is ****wrong / bad / inadequate****."

To pick an answer saying that the main point is "the explanation is still up for debate" insinuates that the author presented this topic in a detached way with no specific preference for which side is right.

choices.text: is extremely complicated
choices.explanation:
We're trying to match our answer choice with "what mirrors do and what happens when we look into mirrors", because that is what the author explicitly says is what's needed for a proper/adequate explanation.

We have no reason to think that encompassing both of those things the author is requiring is *extremely complicated*.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, the left-to-right reversal of objects reflected in mirrors is

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
Well, this was the central question of the passage:
*what causes the left-to-right reversal*?

According to the field-of-sight explanation, it's caused by the fact that we ordinarily rotate our field of sight about a vertical axis (second to last sentence of the 1st paragraph).

According to the front-to-back explanation, it's would be because the reflected image we see is something identical to, and directly facing, itself. If you were facing yourself, your left shoulder would be to your right.

How do we know which explanation to use?

1. only the field-of-sight explanation directly answered the question of why images appear reversed left-to-right. We might infer how front-to-back would answer this question, but the 2nd paragraph never says left-to-right.

2. the author doesn't like the 2nd explanation (front-to-back). So since the author is implying to her reader that this 2nd explanation isn't a valid one, we shouldn't use it as an answer to, "What would this passage say is the reason mirrors behave as they do?"

So let's look for something like the second to last line of the first paragraph.

choices.text: a result of the front-to-back reversal of objects reflected in mirrors
choices.explanation: The author does not endorse this second explanation, nor does the text we read about it ever directly weigh in on why images appear reversed left-to-right.

choices.text: a result of the fact that we ordinarily rotate our field of sight about a vertical axis
choices.explanation:
This is just a verbatim excerpt of the second to last sentence in the first paragraph, which says "Since [answer choice], mirror images usually appear reversed left-to-right".

We might think we're going crazy having an answer be this literal and attached to the keywords in the question stem, but this one just is a direct fact retrieval question.

choices.text: explained by the size and position of the object reflected in the mirror
choices.tag: Out of Scope: size of the object
choices.explanation: Neither explanation ever talks about how big the size of the object is, as a causal factor in why mirror images appear reversed.

choices.text: explained by the difference between two-dimensional and three-dimensional objects
choices.explanation:
The author speaks about how a mirror is a 2-dimensional surface that we perceive 3 dimensionally (in part by adjusting our focal lengths into the imagined space).

But this discussion is only about how mirrors appear to have depth; it isn't connected in any way to why mirror images appear reversed left-to-right.

choices.text: explained by the mental constructs of those who observe objects reflected in mirrors
choices.explanation:
The author speaks about the mental constructs in the 3rd paragraph, saying that mirrors are an unusual case in which our mental construct does not really match objective reality, since we see 3 dimensionality in a 2-dimensional surface.

But this discussion is only about how mirrors appear to have depth; it isn't connected in any way to why mirror images appear reversed left-to-right.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, the fact that we are accustomed to dealing with our mental constructs rather than the primary sense perceptions on which those constructs are based facilitates our ability to

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
The question stem keywords about "accustomed to dealing with our mental constructs" appear in the 2nd sentence of the 3rd paragraph.

This question stem is saying, "Because we're accustomed to constructs not primary perceptions, it *facilitates* ____ ?"

We need to search before / after / inside this sentence for a ****causal**** relationship, where being accustomed to constructs makes something easier or promotes something (*to facilitate =* to make something easier or more conducive).

The causal wording we get is
"*It seems natural* *****because***** *we are accustomed".*
So being accustomed to constructs not perceptions facilitates "it" seeming natural. What is "it"? This pronoun refers to the previous sentence's "this explanation", which refers to the front-to-back explanation.

Okay, so being accustomed to constructs not perceptions facilitates our acceptance of the front-to-back explanation?

Maybe. Are there any causal verbs *after* we start talking about being accustomed to mental constructs rather than perceptions?

Kind of --- it just says that mirrors are one of the few times where our constructs don't match our perceptions. So I guess we could say that being accustomed to constructs not perceptions leaves us vulnerable to being wrong when it comes to mirrors.

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body: Look for something reinforcing that "being accustomed to constructs, not perceptions" is why we naturally accept and find appealing the front-to-back explanation of mirrors, which is a rare disconnect between perception and mental construct.

choices.text: accept the top-to-bottom explanation of what mirrors do
choices.explanation: There isn't ever a top-to-bottom explanation discussed in the passage, just field-of-sight and front-to-back.

choices.text: understand the front-to-back explanation of what mirrors do
choices.explanation:
The 2nd sentence of the 3rd paragraph is saying that "the front-to-back explanation" appeals strongly and seems natural because we're accustomed to dealing with constructs not perceptions.

So being accustomed to dealing with constructs, not perceptions, *facilitates* the natural, intuitive appeal of the front-to-back explanation.

This answer requires that we stretch from "people find it appealing / it seems natural / its intuitive appeal (beginning of 4th paragraph" to the answer choice's phrasing of "facilitates understanding".

It's not a perfect match, but it's the closest we're offered. It's easier to understand something that's intuitive and feels natural than to understand something that's surprising or counterintuitive.

choices.text: challenge complex explanations of common perceptual observations
choices.explanation:
This answer choice is saying that because people are accustomed to dealing with their mental constructs rather than their primary perceptions, they're better able to fight scientists when it comes to challenging the scientists' complex explanation of a perceptual observations?

It's probably fair to say that being accustomed to constructs not perceptions ****increases our likelihood**** of fighting someone with a more challengingly complex explanation of how mirrors work, but that's different from saying ****it helps us to be able to challenge**** complex explanations.

More importantly, the passage is never talking about ordinary people challenging complex explanations. They might find such explanations less intuitively appealing, but nothing here is saying that they actively try to rebut those explanations.

choices.text: reject customarily reliable equations between perceptions and their associated mental constructs
choices.explanation: We're accustomed to dealing with constructs, not perceptions, because we ****accept**** the customarily reliable equation between the two.

choices.text: overemphasize the fact that mirrors simulate sense impressions of objects
choices.explanation:
I don't know where to begin with this word salad.

It's incredibly awkward to say
"X facilitated my ability to overemphasize ... "

Who ever lacks the ability to overemphasize? We're free to overemphasize anything whenever we'd like to. That's free speech.

So that verb is already an answer-killer. But could we even say that "it's a fact that mirrors simulate sense impressions of objects"?

No, that doesn't make any sense either. Maybe an artificial intelligence computer could simulate sense impressions.

Mirrors are an object that provide us cognitive beings with our sense impressions. They aren't simulating sense impressions. Because our perception / mental construct of the image in a mirror is one with depth, we could say that our mental construct of what we're seeing is simulating depth when it perceives the mirror's surface.

Taking a big step back, this answer seems to even say the opposite of what the passage is saying.

Because we deal with constructs not perceptions, we find the front-to-back explanation naturally appealing, which means we're ****under-****emphasizing or failing to recognize that we're only pretending / simulating the idea that images in mirrors have depth.

questions.prompt: It can be inferred that the author of the passage believes that the front-to-back explanation of what mirrors do is

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
How does our author feel about the front-to-back?

Well the main point was essentially all about ****Challenging**** this ****Position****. The author's final two sentences are where she takes down the front-to-back and makes it seem like an "improper" answer to questions about the appearance of images, since it doesn't factor the observer into its explanation.

The author *did* pepper in some niceties along the way:

The beginning of the 3rd says
*This explanation appeals strongly to many people, however, because it is quite successful at explaining what a mirror does -- to a point*.

And in the beginning of the 4th paragraph,
*In addition to its* *****intuitive appeal******, the front-to-back explanation is motivated in part by the traditional desire in science to ...*

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body:
So putting that all together we'd say the author thinks the front-to-back is
- successful to a point
- intuitively appealing
- aligned with a traditional desire of science
- ****but,**** not a proper answer to the question about the appearances of images in a mirror

choices.text: successful because it is based on incongruous facts that can be reconciled
choices.explanation:
The author's main point is that the front to back is not an adequate explanation, so calling the theory ****successful**** seems to go agains the author's main thrust.

She certainly doesn't mention that it reconciles incongruous facts.

choices.text: successful because it rejects any consideration of mental constructs
choices.explanation:
The author's main point is that the front to back is not an adequate explanation because it fails to consider the observer (the person with the mental constructs), so this seems like the opposite.

The author would be more likely to call it ****unsuccessful**** because it's rejecting any consideration of the observer.

choices.text: successful because it involves the rotation of a field of sight about an axis
choices.explanation:
*Rotating a field of sight* was not part of "front-to-back". It was part of the aptly named "field of sight" explanation.

So this answer is saying "The 2nd theory is successful because it says what the 1st theory said".

choices.text: successful only to a point because it is consistent with the traditional explanations that physicists have offered
choices.explanation:
"Successful only to a point" is supported by the first sentence of the 3rd paragraph:

*it is quite successful at explaining what a mirror does -- to a point*.

But the reason the author won't give this explanation full credit is because of what is said in the final two sentences of the passage.

When we say, "It was successful only to a point because ....", the thing we would naturally insert in that spot of the sentence is the factor that ****prevented**** it from being a total success.

The author never said that front-to-back was prevented from being fully successful because it's consistent with traditional explanations.

choices.text: successful only to a point because it does not include what happens when we look into a mirror
choices.explanation:
"Successful only to a point" is supported by the first sentence of the 3rd paragraph:

*it is quite successful at explaining what a mirror does -- to a point*.

The reason the author won't give this explanation full credit is because of what is said in the final two sentences of the passage:

*if we don't consider both what mirrors do* *****and what happens when we look into mirrors******, then questions about the appearances of images cannot be properly answered.*

questions.prompt: In the passage the author is primarily concerned with doing which one of the following?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
This passage seems to mainly be a Challenge a Position type passage.

After introducing the "standard" explanation, in the first paragraph, for why the image of an object is reversed in a mirror, the author brings up a "different" explanation in the 2nd paragraph.

In the 3rd paragraph, the author acknowledges the appeal of / motivation behind this different explanation, and then in the 4th paragraph, he explains why he doesn't consider it an acceptable explanation (because it removes the *observer* from a conversation about *appearances*).

choices.text: evaluating the experimental evidence for and against two diametrically opposed explanations of a given phenomenon
choices.explanation: There are no experiments referred to in this passage. The author is comparing two explanations of a given phenomenon, but we don't look at experiments conducted by both sides.

choices.text: demonstrating that different explanations of the same phenomenon are based on different empirical observations
choices.explanation:
The empirical observations people have about mirrors flipping things aren't different. We all see images flipped in the mirror. We're all making the same observation.

Also, this answer choice sounds like it's legitimizing both explanations (hey, they're just coming from different observational evidence), but the passage doesn't think the 2nd explanation is legit.

choices.text: describing the difficulties that must be overcome if a satisfactory explanation of a phenomenon is to be found
choices.explanation:
This answer makes it sound like the author is unhappy with both explanations presented and is ending the passage saying, "As you can see, we still don't have a satisfactory explanation -- here's what we would need in order to get one."

But the author seems implicitly satisfied with the explanation in the first paragraph. She never pushes back against it. That explanation isn't vulnerable to the objection she's making at the end of the 4th paragraph. That objection is only for the 2nd explanation.

choices.text: showing why one explanation of a phenomenon falls short in explaining the phenomenon
choices.explanation:
This sounds the most like a ****Challenge a Position**** type purpose. The author presents the standard explanation for reversed images in mirrors, then Purpose Pivots (but, yet, ****however****, recently) into this 2nd explanation.

After explaining it, then discussing the appeal of it and the motives behind it, she ends with why it isn't a satisfactory explanation.

choices.text: relating the theoretical support for an explanation of a phenomenon to the acceptance of that explanation
choices.tag: Too Narrow / Out of Scope: theoretical support
choices.explanation:
In the 3rd paragraph, the author is getting into the subject matter of how the intuitive appeal of the 2nd phenomenon makes people want to accept it, and how the motivation to remove the observer from physical explanations makes physicists want to accept it. But this is not the main purpose of the passage.

Also, we don't really ever talk about "theoretical *support*" for either explanation (we kinda just hear what each explanation is), and we don't connect theoretical support to acceptance.

questions.prompt: With which one of the following statements would the author of the passage be most likely to agree?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
All the question stem gives us to go off of is "author", so we can ask ourselves if we remember specific moments where the author's voice cut through, or just remind ourselves of the main point.

The author's main point was that this "front-to-back" explanation is not a "proper answer" to the question about appearances of images, because "how an image appears" entails that there is an observer to observe how it appears, and the front-to-back explanation removes the observer from consideration.

The other two moments where we hear the author's voice is when she is making concessions to the front-to-back explanation that she will ultimately trash:

- Beginning of 3rd paragraph: *this explanation appeals strongly to many people because* *****it is quite successful***** *at explaining what a mirror does --* *****to a point******.*

That's giving partial credit to the front-to-back explanation.

- Beginning of 4th paragraph: *in addition to intuitive appeal, front-to-back is* *****motivated in part by the traditional desire***** *in science to separate the observer from the phenomenon.*

The author is saying, "even though I'm going to complain in a sec about how this explanation removes the observer from consideration, I feel ya -- I know that traditionally in science we want to separate the observer."

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body: Look for something safely worded that we can support with some line(s) from the passage.

choices.text: The failure of one recent explanation of what mirrors do illustrates the need for better optical equipment in future experiments with mirrors.
choices.tag: Too Strong: the need / Out of Scope: better optical equipment
choices.explanation:
The author never indicates having any issue with the field-of-sight explanation, so the fact that the author thinks the front-to-back explanation fails doesn't mean we ****need**** to do anything.

We could just believe the explanation that *doesn't* leave out the observer. We certainly have no grounds for saying the author is agitating for better optical equipment.

choices.text: Explanations of what mirrors do generally fail because physicists overlook the differences between objects and reflections of objects.
choices.explanation: We only have one instance (front-to-back) of an explanation of what mirrors do failing. We can't inflate that into, "Yup ... this thing ****usually**** happens".

choices.text: One explanation of what mirrors do reveals the traditional tendency of physicists to separate a phenomenon to be explained from the observer of the phenomenon.
choices.explanation:
Yes, this is supported by the first sentence of the final paragraph.

(Beginning of 4th paragraph)
*in addition to intuitive appeal, the front-to-back explanation is* *****motivated in part by the traditional desire***** *in science to separate the observer from the phenomenon.*

choices.text: The degree to which human beings tend to deal directly with mental constructs rather than with primary sense perceptions depends on their training in the sciences.
choices.explanation:
In the 3rd paragraph, the author says "we (all humans) are accustomed to dealing with our mental constructs of objects rather than with the primary sense perceptions".

She never qualifies that and say, "That is, unless you've had a lot of training in the sciences, in which case you deal more with primary sense perceptions".

She doesn't make any connection between how much science training we've had and how much we deal with mental construct rather than primary sense perception.

choices.text: Considering objects reflected in mirrors to be mental constructs interferes with an accurate understanding of how primary perceptions function.
choices.explanation:
This answer is just taking lots of different words and phrases from the passage and tossing them together. It's hard to find an offending word (other than "interferes"). It's just the overall meaning of the sentence isn't close to anything the author ever said.

The passage is never talking about whether or not we have an *accurate understanding of how primary perceptions function*.

That's way too broad, when we are only talking about mirrors. The author is just shooting down an explanation for why the images in mirrors appear reversed. She's never complaining that how we think about mirrors disrupts our ability to have an accurate understanding about how our primary perceptions (sight / sound / taste / smell / touch) function.

questions.prompt: The author would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements about the field-of-sight explanation of what mirrors do?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
We know our author appreciates the appeal of front-to-back but ultimately thinks it's an inadequate explanation, because it doesn't involve the observer, which should be necessary to any explanation to how mirrors *appear to the viewer*.

The author doesn't directly editorialize how she feels about field-of-sight, but we know that field-of-sight would not be vulnerable to the same criticism; it *does* reference the role of the observer.

Beyond that, the author seems to think of field-of-sight as the "standard" answer from physicists, and since she never pushes back against it, she's probably pretty sympathetic to it.

choices.text: This explanation is based on the traditional desire of physicists to simplify the explanation of what mirrors do.
choices.explanation:
This answer sounds more like how the author described the front-to-back explanation (the 3rd paragraph is saying that front-to-back has intuitive appeal because it basically validates our fraudulent mental constructs about mirrors).

I know when I read this passage, I had a way simpler time understanding the front-to-back than I did the field-of-sight.

choices.text: This explanation does not depend on the false premise that images in mirrors have three-dimensional properties.
choices.explanation:
At the end of the 2nd paragraph, the author said, "****the most** ***notable***** (i.e. special / unique) thing about this explanation is that it's based on a false premise that the object in the mirror is three dimensional."

Since the author singles out that characteristic about the front-to-back explanation, we can infer that this characteristic is not shared by field-of-sight.

For example, no one would say, "There are two main candidates for President: Biden and Trump. The most notable thing about Trump is that he's an old white guy." because Biden is also an old white guy.

choices.text: This explanation fails to take into account the point of view and orientation of someone who is observing reflections in the mirror.
choices.explanation: The field-of-sight is explicitly about the point of view and orientation of someone observing reflections!

choices.text: This explanation assumes that people who see something in a mirror do not understand the reality of what they see.
choices.explanation: Neither explanation assumes that people don't understand the reality of what they see.

choices.text: This explanation is unsuccessful because it involves claims about how people rotate their field of sight rather than claims about what people can imagine.
choices.explanation: The author thinks this is a more successful explanation, since it actually takes into account the observer who is observing the images/appearances of things in the mirror.

questions.prompt: The author mentions the fact that we rarely focus our eyes on mirrors (near the end of the third paragraph) primarily in order to

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
This is a Local Purpose question, which uses language like *serves to / primarily to / in order to*. The correct answer to these is usually reinforcing the bigger claim that comes right before (or sometimes right after) the detail we're being asked about in the question stem.

The last sentence of the 3rd paragraph, where this question stem is pointing us, even says ****for example****, so we know the rhetorical purpose of this final sentence is to illustrate the claim made in the previous sentence.

The overall point of that paragraph was that mirrors are a weird exception where our perceptions don't exactly match their associated mental constructs.

The way we construe our sense perceptions of a mirror is contrary to fact. They're designed to make a 2D surface appear to have depth.

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body: Bringing up that mirrors are among ****the few**** objects on which we don't focus our eyes is a callback / illustration of the previous claim that mirrors are ****an exception**** to the standard correspondence between perception and mental construct.

choices.text: contrast our capacity to perceive objects with our capacity to imagine objects
choices.explanation:
We are talking about artificially believing that there's a person "in the mirror" standing as far behind its surface as we are standing in front of it.

But we're not quite imagining objects. Those objects are in the room with us. We're just perceiving their appearance in the mirror in a way that is contrary to fact.

choices.text: emphasize that it is impossible to perceive reflected objects without using mental constructs of the objects
choices.explanation:
The author is never saying anything as strong as, "it is ****impossible**** to perceive a reflected object without using mental constructs".

We can't find any supporting text that has wording that extreme.

choices.text: clarify the idea that mirrors simulate three-dimensional reality
choices.explanation:
This reinforces the 2nd to last sentence of the 3rd paragraph. We know the function of the last sentence of the 3rd is ****an example**** to illustrate what was said in the 2nd to last.

So we should be happy to see an answer choice saying, "it was there to illustrate what we were saying in the 2nd to last sentence".

That's just what this does. That 2nd to last sentence said:

*mirrors are "designed" to make a two-dimensional surface appear to have depth (i.e. appear to have three-dimensions)*. *For example, we don't focus our eyes on them. (meaning, we look* *****into***** *them as though they have depth*.

Again, the general formula for Local Purpose questions is to find an answer that sounds like the sentence / bigger claim that came right before the detail the question stem is asking about.

choices.text: illustrate the fact that we typically deal directly with mental constructs rather than with perceptions
choices.explanation:
Saying that *we don't focus our eyes on the surface of a mirror* wasn't trying to illustrate that we typically deal with mental constructs.

If fact, this line tells us that mirrors are ****among the few**** objects where we *don't* focus our eyes on them. So this is illustrating something ****a****typical, not typical.

choices.text: emphasize the degree to which the psychological activity of the observer modifies the shape of the object being perceived
choices.explanation:
Not focusing our eyes on the surface of a mirror doesn't quite match the term "psychological activity" (like thought / emotion).

We don't exert voluntary control over our focal length. That would be like calling *blinking* a psychological activity.
